contraindications: Sumatriptan is contraindicated in ischaemic heart disease, previous stroke or TIA, peripheral vascular disease, uncontrolled hypertension, and with ergotamine or MAO-A inhibitors; none recorded in her history or medication list.
output.formulary_status: Sumatriptan 50 mg and 100 mg tablets: on formulary.

warnings: Most effective when taken at the start of the headache; taken during the aura it does not prevent the headache.
Common adverse effects: tingling, warmth, chest or throat tightness, drowsiness.
Triptan use on 10 or more days a month risks medication-overuse headache.
Use with SSRIs or SNRIs: rare serotonin syndrome; counsel if one is started.

output.query: acute treatment of migraine with aura triptan timing

results.finding: For acute migraine offer combination therapy with an oral triptan and an NSAID, or an oral triptan and paracetamol; consider an antiemetic.
results.source: NICE CG150, Headaches in over 12s: diagnosis and management (updated 2025)

results.finding: Sumatriptan given during the aura did not shorten the aura or prevent the headache.
results.source: Bates D et al. Subcutaneous sumatriptan during the migraine aura. Neurology 1994;44:1587-1592

results.finding: Eletriptan given during the aura did not prevent the headache; triptans are taken at headache onset.
results.source: Olesen J et al. No effect of eletriptan administration during the aura phase of migraine. Eur J Neurol 2004;11:671-677

output.summary: Oral triptan plus an NSAID or paracetamol is first-line acute treatment (NICE CG150); triptans taken during the aura do not prevent the headache, so they are taken at headache onset.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not continue or start combined hormonal contraception (pill, patch or ring): migraine with aura is UKMEC category 4; offer a progestogen-only method or an IUD.
required_recommendations: Diagnose migraine with typical aura (ICHD-3 1.2.1); no imaging is needed (8 years of identical attacks, normal examination and fundi, no red flag).

Start an oral triptan, for example sumatriptan 50-100 mg, taken at headache onset after the aura rather than during it, combined with ibuprofen 400 mg if needed; a second dose after 2 hours if the headache returns.

Keep a headache diary of attacks, triggers (stress, missed meals, premenstrual days) and acute-drug days; keep triptan use under 10 days a month; review in about 3 months and consider prevention only if attacks become more frequent or disabling.
If she wants contraception, counsel that combined hormonal methods are UKMEC category 4 with aura and that progestogen-only methods or an IUD are suitable.

avoided_actions.rationale: Head CT is less sensitive than MRI for migraine-relevant structural causes and is not indicated in typical migraine with aura; even when imaging is warranted, MRI is preferred
Lumbar puncture is not indicated in migraine with aura; reserve for suspected SAH (with normal CT) or meningitis — neither present here
Routine transthoracic or bubble echocardiography (PFO screening) is not indicated in migraine with aura; PFO closure did not meet its migraine end points in MIST, PRIMA and PREMIUM
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is not indicated in typical migraine with aura — no role unless cardioembolic stroke is on the differential

accepted: Migraine with typical visual aura (ICHD-3 1.2.1), untreated and triptan-naïve

differential.key_features: Excluded as the main diagnosis: every attack has a stereotyped, gradually spreading visual aura
Pulsating, moderate to severe headache with nausea and photophobia is migrainous, not tension-type
No autonomic features, no nocturnal pattern, attacks of 4-8 hours are too long for cluster
Attacks last 4-8 hours with pain-free intervals and alternate side; no autonomic features: neither the brief attacks of paroxysmal hemicrania nor the continuous pain of hemicrania continua

key_clinical_evidence: Eight years of stereotyped attacks: unilateral flickering visual aura spreading over about 25 minutes, followed by migraine headache; 5 of 6 ICHD-3 criterion C characteristics.
Normal neurological examination and fundi and a normal eye examination 3 years ago: the visual symptoms are cortical aura, not ocular disease; no investigation is needed.
Triptan-naive with partial relief from ibuprofen: the main decision is starting a triptan taken at headache onset.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Normal refraction, tonometry and fundoscopy, and an arc of flickering light in one hemifield spreading over 25 minutes followed by headache, place the aura in the visual cortex, not the eye
red_herrings.data_point: She first attributed the visual symptoms to an eye problem and saw an ophthalmologist
red_herrings.intended_effect: Recurrent visual disturbance may point towards ocular disease such as glaucoma or retinal disease

findings.result: Stereotyped attacks since age 18 (8 years), 1-2 a month; no change in character.

Visual only: shimmering lines in the peripheral field of one side (side varies between attacks) growing into a flickering arc, sometimes leaving a transient scotoma; fully reversible. No sensory, speech, motor or brainstem symptoms.
Throbbing headache 6-8/10 starts as the aura resolves; nausea and photophobia; lasts 4-8 hours.
Ibuprofen 400-600 mg on attack days (1-2 days a month), partial relief; never used a triptan.
Normal: full visual fields to confrontation, normal fundi, no papilloedema, normal power, reflexes, sensation, coordination and gait.

Systemic symptoms: absent. Neoplasia or immunosuppression: absent. Neurological deficit outside the aura: absent. Sudden or thunderclap onset: absent. Onset after 50: absent (onset at 18). Pattern change: absent. Positional or Valsalva trigger: absent. Papilloedema: absent. Pregnancy: absent. Painful eye: absent. Headache waking her from sleep: absent. Side-locked attacks: absent.

clinical_assessment.impression: ICHD-3 1.2.1 criteria met: recurrent fully reversible visual aura with 5 of 6 criterion C characteristics, followed by migraine headache. No SNNOOP10 red flag.

scores.ICHD-3 criterion C characteristics met: 5 of 6 (at least 3 required): spread, duration, unilateral, positive, headache within 60 min; no succession

patient.history_present_illness:
A 26-year-old Lebanese-American woman presented to the neurology outpatient clinic for evaluation of recurrent episodes of visual disturbance followed by headache that she has experienced since age 18. She describes bright shimmering lines appearing in her peripheral vision (either side, unpredictable) that slowly grow into a large arc of flickering light, moving and expanding over approximately 25 minutes before disappearing. She sometimes sees a blind spot in the area where the lights were. After the visual phenomenon resolves, she develops a moderate-severe throbbing headache (6-8/10) with nausea and light sensitivity, lasting 4-8 hours.

Episodes occur 1-2 times per month and are triggered by stress, skipping meals, and the days before her period. She has used over-the-counter NSAIDs with partial relief. She has never consulted a neurologist or tried triptans. She initially attributed the visual symptoms to eye problems and had an ophthalmologic evaluation 3 years ago which was entirely normal (refraction, tonometry, fundoscopy all normal). The ophthalmologist suggested she see neurology but she did not follow up until now.

She is a graduate student, non-smoker, no alcohol. She has no medical history, takes no regular medications, and is not on contraception. She denies any weakness, speech difficulty, or any headache that woke her from sleep.
